openers.title: The Rubbing Alcohol Chill
openers.question: Dab rubbing alcohol on one arm and water on the other. The alcohol feels colder and dries much faster. A vapor monitor reads far higher over the alcohol. What are the alcohol molecules doing, compared with water molecules, that lets them escape into vapor so easily?
openers.model_answer: Alcohol molecules have weaker intermolecular attractions than water, so a larger fraction of particles can overcome cohesive forces at room temperature to evaporate.
openers.target: Intermolecular force strength dictating relative vapor pressure and volatility

media.image_alt: Two panels. Left: a student dabs rubbing alcohol on her arm, shivers, and a vapor monitor reads very high. Right: the same student dabs water, her arm stays wet, and the monitor reads low. A box labelled The Science is blanked out until you answer.

openers.title: The Syringe Boiling Trick
openers.question: You pull some warm water into a plastic syringe. You cap the tip so no air can get in. Then you pull the plunger back hard. The water starts to boil in your hand. You did not heat it. What are the water molecules doing that lets the water boil without heat?
openers.model_answer: Water molecules at the surface keep escaping into vapor. At this temperature they have a set vapor pressure. Pulling the plunger lowers the external pressure on the water. When that external pressure falls to the water's vapor pressure, molecules inside the liquid can escape into bubbles of vapor, so the water boils. The molecules already have enough energy; no heat is added.
openers.target: Boiling happens when the external pressure on a liquid falls to its vapor pressure; vapor pressure depends on temperature

media.image_alt: Two hands hold a large plastic syringe, tip up. The tip is sealed with a short rubber tube and a small capped plastic tube. A thin layer of water sits between the tip and the plunger's dark rubber seal. Small bubbles show in the water. The plunger rod runs down through the barrel into the hands.
media.credit: Photo: 郭又鑫, CC BY-SA 3.0 https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0 via Wikimedia Commons https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Boiling_hot_water_below_100_deg_C_under_1atm_environment.JPG

openers.title: The Drinking Bird
openers.question: A toy bird sits beside a cup of water. You wet the felt on its head. Soon it tips forward, dips its beak in the water, and swings back up. It does this again and again. It has no battery and no spring. What are the molecules doing, on the wet head and inside the sealed glass, that keeps the bird moving?
openers.model_answer: Water molecules on the wet felt evaporate; the most energetic ones leave cooling the head. Inside the sealed glass, the cooler head has a lower vapor pressure than the warm body: vapor condenses on the cold glass, and fewer molecules escape from the cold liquid. The higher vapor pressure in the warm body pushes liquid up the neck. The top grows heavy and the bird tips.
openers.target: Vapor pressure depends on temperature; a temperature difference inside a sealed container makes a pressure difference that can move liquid

media.image_alt: Video, 35 seconds, silent. Two toy drinking birds stand on either side of a paper cup of water. Each has a glass body holding colored liquid, a long glass neck, and a felt head with a top hat. Liquid rises up a bird's neck, the bird tips forward, dips its beak in the cup, and swings back up. They take turns.
media.credit: Video: חזרתי, CC BY 4.0 https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0 via Wikimedia Commons https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:DrinkingBird1.webm ; adapted: caption added, trimmed

openers.title: The Deep-Sea Vent
openers.question: Far down on the sea floor, very hot water pours out of a rock chimney. A probe in the stream reads hotter than a pizza oven. Yet no steam bubbles form. At vents in shallower water, the hot water fizzes. What are the water molecules doing that keeps the deep water from boiling?
openers.model_answer: Water molecules in the hot stream move fast, and many have enough energy to escape into vapor. But a bubble can only form if the vapor inside it pushes back as hard as the water pressing on it. Deep down, the weight of the water above squeezes the molecules together and keeps them from spreading apart into vapor. That pressure is very large, so the water must be much hotter before its vapor pressure is high enough to open a bubble. In shallower water the pressure is lower, so the water reaches its boiling point at a lower temperature, and it fizzes.
openers.target: Boiling happens when the vapor pressure reaches the pressure on the liquid; more pressure means a higher boiling point

media.image_alt: Video, 21 seconds, with the sound of the vent. Deep-sea footage from a remotely operated vehicle. Pale mineral chimneys rise from the dark sea floor. Cloudy plumes pour from their tops and drift away. Close up, a thin white stream jets from an opening in the rock. Pale crabs and shrimp crowd the chimney walls. A caption reads MARIANIS TRENCH HYDROTHERMAL VENTS.
media.credit: Video: NOAA, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:0501-hydrothermal-vents-640x360.webm ; adapted: trimmed, caption added
